faq.a: Tumours with high turnover release more LDH; higher levels correlate with aggressive disease and lower survival.
faq.q: Why is LDH used for cancer prognosis?

faq.a: No; many conditions (early infection, small tumours) may have normal LDH. Use it with other clinical data.
faq.q: Can a normal LDH rule out serious disease?

faq.a: It prompts a focused search for hidden haemolysis, occult malignancy, or organ infarction.

exam: Explain how LDH is incorporated into lymphoma staging and what a level >2 × ULN implies.
List three common causes of elevated LDH in a low‑resource setting and the key test to differentiate each.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is an enzyme released from damaged cells. Elevated levels signal tissue injury, high tumour turnover, or haemolysis and help gauge disease severity.

b: Elevated LDH indicates cell membrane disruption or rapid cell turnover.
Low LDH is rare and usually not clinically important.
sections.p: LDH is a cytoplasmic enzyme present in most organs. Serum measurement uses a colourimetric assay; normal adult range is roughly 140‑280 U/L, but labs vary.

b: LDH >2 × ULN often moves a patient to a higher risk category.
Serial rise suggests disease progression.
sections.p: In oncology, LDH is incorporated into staging systems (e.g., International Prognostic Index for lymphoma, AJCC for melanoma). Higher multiples of the upper limit of normal (ULN) correlate with poorer prognosis.

b: 1️⃣ Haemolysis (malaria, sickle‑cell crisis, G6PD deficiency).
2️⃣ Tissue necrosis (myocardial infarction, severe sepsis, trauma).
3️⃣ High tumour burden (lymphoma, leukemia, germ‑cell tumours).
4️⃣ Hepatitis B or C with liver injury.
5️⃣ Tuberculosis with extensive organ involvement.
sections.p: LDH rises from any condition that damages cells or increases turnover. In low‑resource settings, common causes include infections, haemolysis, and malignancy.

b: Often discovered incidentally on routine labs.
May accompany other abnormal markers (AST, bilirubin, CK).
sections.p: LDH itself is asymptomatic; clinicians notice it when evaluating unexplained fatigue, jaundice, chest pain, or when staging a known cancer.
LDH is a screening tool; further tests pinpoint the source of injury.

t.a: Complete blood count with peripheral smear
t.b: Is haemolysis or marrow infiltration present? → Schistocytes or blasts confirm cause.
Is haemolysis the driver? → Low haptoglobin, high indirect bilirubin support.
Is myocardial injury responsible? → Elevated troponin confirms infarction.
Is there tumour or organ necrosis? → Mass or infarct explains LDH rise.

b: Acute tumour lysis syndrome (hyperuricaemia, renal failure).
Severe haemolytic crisis causing acute kidney injury.
Massive myocardial infarction with cardiogenic shock.
sections.p: Very high LDH (>5 × ULN) often signals rapid cell death that can lead to organ failure.

b: Oncologic disease → chemotherapy, targeted therapy; LDH guides intensity.
Haemolysis → treat infection (antimalarials, antibiotics), transfuse if needed, avoid oxidant drugs.
Myocardial infarction → reperfusion, antiplatelet agents, beta‑blockers; LDH trends monitor reperfusion success.
Tumour lysis syndrome → aggressive hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase, monitor electrolytes.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause; supportive care targets complications.

b: Check LDH every 1‑2 weeks during active cancer therapy.
In chronic haemolysis, monitor quarterly and adjust disease‑modifying therapy.
Educate patients on avoiding triggers (e.g., certain drugs in G6PD deficiency).
sections.p: Serial LDH measurements track response and detect early relapse.

b: Creatine kinase (CK) – muscle‑specific, rises in rhabdomyolysis.
AST – liver and cardiac enzyme, may parallel LDH but is organ‑specific.
sections.p: Other enzymes that rise with tissue injury can be mistaken for LDH.

b: Hemolysed blood sample can artificially raise LDH.
Mild elevation in pregnancy or strenuous exercise may be benign.
Low LDH does not exclude disease if the source releases other markers.
sections.p: LDH is non‑specific; interpretation must consider clinical context.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain with high LDH suggests myocardial infarction.
Rapid LDH rise >5 × ULN with renal failure points to tumour lysis or severe haemolysis.
Severe malaria with LDH >3 × ULN and altered mental status requires urgent care.
